newsitem.title: USA: Levitt-Blue ribbon panel pushes end to pay-to-play.
newsitem.headline: Levitt-Blue ribbon panel pushes end to pay-to-play.

text.p: SEC Chairman Arthur Levitt on Thursday announced formation of a panel of "legal luminaries" headed by former CIA chief William Webster to push for end to the "odious" practice of pay-to-play.

"A few weeks ago, several of the leading lawyers in our nation gathered in my office ... because they found pay-to-play an odious, obnoxious practice and wished to say so publicly," Levitt told attendees at a Fixed Income Daily conference on muni finance, according to a prepared speech.

"They felt that more should be done to end the practice - and that, if given the chance, many of their colleagues would agree. These legal luminaries have organized 'The Lawyers' Committee to End Pay-to-Play,'" the Securities and Exchange Commission's chief said, according to the written speech.
Pay-to-play refers to municipal bond professionals who give contributions to elected municipal officials in return for a crack at bond business.

Wall Street bond dealers four years ago signed a voluntary pact banning pay-to-play among their ranks. Levitt has aggressively pushed bond lawyers, who are not directly regulated by the SEC, to do the same.

"Where are the lawyers?" Levitt asked Thursday. "I am sorry to have to report to you that, as of today, no meaningful nationwide measure has been put in place by our country's lawyers to stop, or even slow down, 'pay-to-play.' "
The American Bar Association is expected to take a key vote this August on whether to adopt a controversial pay-to-play ban developed by New York City's bar.
The ban would prohibit muni lawyers that solicit or contribute to muni clients from doing bond business for two years with those governments.

Levitt said that the new lawyers' committee also will include former Attorney General Elliot Richardson, former SEC Commissioner Steve Freidman, and such "noted" securities lawyers as James Doty, Michael Halloran, John Lifton, Jack Levin and John Olson.
Webster, former Central Intelligence Agency chief and former U.S. Judge for the Eastern District of Missouri, was not available for comment.

Webster's panel is expected to urge local, state and national bar associations to condemn pay-to-play practices by muni bond lawyers. The group is not expected to call for a flat ban on contributions, however.
Meanwhile, ABA panels are developing alternatives to the New York City bar's resolution that are not as tough and that they hope will sell with ABA delegates in August.

ABA's standing committee on professional discipline adopted a statement that "decries" pay-to-play and "encourages state legislatures and other regulatory agencies to adopt appropriate rules and policies" on the issue.

And a broad panel representing seven ABA committees and sections called for a task force to study the issue and report back to ABA delegates in August 1998. The task force would examine pay-to-play among all lawyers - not just muni lawyers - including gifts to judges.
